role: Driver of control I: the part L line twice, each from an idle machine.
purpose: go2.sh runs the part L line (`like.spec`) two more times through `rx.sh`. Before each of the two processes it waits until the 1-minute load average is below 1.0.

main_flow.step: Set `set -u`, the paths on CRB, the two expected sha256 values and the expected boot id (the same values as in go.sh).
Define the helpers `state` (prints one state line) and `fail` (prints the reason and ends the run with exit status 1).
Print the process id of go2.sh.
Run the checks: marker file, lock file, sha256 of `rx.sh` and of bwx12, presence of `like.spec`, boot id, MemTotal. Each failed check calls `fail`.
Define `rxok` (tests the `rc` line that `rx.sh` wrote) and `waitidle` (waits at most 15 min for a 1-minute load average below 1.0).
Twice: wait for an idle machine, print a state line, run `rx.sh` with `like.spec` (names `T72I1` and `T72I2`), test the `rc` line, print a state line.
Print the last state line and `ALLDONE`.

behavior_notes: go2.sh measures nothing itself. It reads no clock for a rate and computes no rate. All timed intervals are inside the binary bwx12. While bwx12 runs, go2.sh only waits for `rx.sh`.

`Idle` is a rule on the 1-minute load average only. In the rerun the two `idle before` state lines show 1-minute values of 0.95 and 0.99. The 5-minute values in the same two lines are 36.39 and 21.40 [Ref1].

bwx12 does not start at the idle test. `rx.sh` first waits until at most 2 tasks are runnable, and then 5 s more [Ref2]. In the rerun the two launch lines (22:27:05 and 22:32:32) are 5 s after the two idle state lines (22:27:00 and 22:32:27). The launch lines show 1-minute load averages of 0.87 and 0.91 [Ref1] [Ref6].

Time since the 120-thread work before, in the rerun: the first control process started 287 s after the end of the last process of go.sh (22:22:18 to 22:27:05). The second started 265 s after the end of the first (22:28:07 to 22:32:32). These are the times of the `rc` lines and the `launch` lines [Ref6].
A failed check stops the whole run with exit status 1 (function `fail`, line 14). go2.sh uses the lock file of go.sh. So it cannot run while go.sh runs.
go2.sh does not print the Linux kernel command line, the governors, the huge page settings or the CPU list of its shell. go.sh prints them [Ref9].

How go2.sh was started on CRB: no script of the run folder holds the command. An AI agent (Claude Code) ran the rerun. Its transcript (the saved record of its commands and their outputs) holds the command [Ref10]. The agent sent one command line from its server to CRB with `ssh` (the remote login tool), as the user `jhan`. The part that starts go2.sh reads: `L=~/cache-perf/results/go2-T72-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).log; nohup setsid ~/cache-perf/w120-7200-20261117/go2.sh > $L 2>&1 < /dev/null &`.

What the start command sets: `> $L 2>&1` sends the standard output and the error output of go2.sh to the log file [Ref1]. go2.sh itself names no log file. `< /dev/null` gives go2.sh an empty input. `nohup` starts go2.sh with the hangup signal ignored. The hangup signal tells a program that its terminal or connection was closed. `setsid` makes go2.sh the leader of a new process group [Ref11]. So the `kill` command that line 15 prints reaches go2.sh and its child processes.

Insufficient data: the CPU list of the shell of go2.sh in the rerun. The start command holds no `taskset` [Ref10]. go2.sh does not print the list. A line `taskset -cp $$` in go2.sh would resolve it for a later run. For comparison: the start command of go.sh had the same form [Ref10]. It ran about 11 min earlier in the same boot. The log of go.sh shows the list `0-119` for its shell [Ref12].

Is the local go2.sh the script that ran: the log of go2.sh and the files that the run wrote to its result folders hold no checksum of go2.sh. The transcript holds the command that copied the files to CRB [Ref13]. The agent wrote go2.sh on its server and wrote its sha256 to the file `go2.sha`. It copied both files to CRB. There `sha256sum -c go2.sha` printed `go2.sh: OK`, about 5 s before the start command. The transcript holds no command of the agent between this test and the start command. The local go2.sh still has the sha256 of `go2.sha` (tested with `sha256sum -c` on 2026-11-21) [Ref14].

What `users` in a state line shows: the number of lines that `who` prints. After the start of go2.sh the start command waited on CRB for the end of go2.sh (`wait $pid`). Then it printed the exit status and the log [Ref10]. So the `ssh` connection of the start command was open during the whole run. All 6 state lines show `users 0` [Ref1]. So `who` did not list this connection. `users 0` does not show that no connection to CRB was open.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17, run after the memory speed was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
one DIMM. CRB has 12 slots.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
a process is one start of a benchmark binary.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the arguments of one bwx12 process, as a spec file holds them. "The same line" means a process with the same arguments.
a launch at a 1-minute load average below 1.0.
a text file that `rx.sh` reads as its input. Each line is `tag|arguments of the binary` and gives one process. The tag becomes the name of the csv file of that process.
a text file whose lines hold values separated by commas.
a line that go.sh or go2.sh prints with the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the load, the logins and the processes per user.

the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. The scripts of this test stop when it exists. The messages of go2.sh, `ra.sh` and `rx.sh` do not say what the file stands for. None of the scripts that test the file says who creates it. Since 2026-11-24 the message in line 20 of go.sh says what the file stands for: Jeremy or someone else is using CRB. Jeremy is another user of CRB. The page `go.sh.md` in this folder (the explanation of go.sh) names the notes that say this. The facts sheet of the rerun says that another user creates it during a performance test [Ref8].
a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.

the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file `/proc/loadavg`). The fourth field of the file gives the tasks that are runnable now and the number of all tasks, for example `1/1013` [Ref7].
the number before the slash in the fourth field of `/proc/loadavg`: the processes and threads that are runnable at the moment of the reading [Ref7].
the Linux policy that sets the CPU frequency.
a Linux feature that can place a buffer on 2 MiB pages.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
the number that a process returns when it ends. 0 means success. `launches.txt` writes it as `rc`.

`launches.txt` is a file that `rx.sh` writes in each of its result folders. `rx.sh` appends a `launch` line directly before it starts a process: the tag, the time, the content of `/proc/loadavg`, the number of logins and the arguments. It appends an `rc` line after the process has ended: the exit status, the tag and the time.
the number that Linux gives to a process.
a set of processes that one signal can reach together. The group has the process id of its leader as its number.
the number under which a process holds an open file.
the CPUs on which Linux may run a process (its CPU affinity).
a Linux tool. `taskset -c 0-119 COMMAND` starts a command that may run on the CPUs 0 to 119 only. `taskset -cp PID` prints the CPU list of a running process.
the command line that started go2.sh on CRB. It is not part of a script. An AI agent (Claude Code) ran the rerun, and the saved record of its commands holds this command line [Ref10].
Coordinated Universal Time. All times of the run are written in UTC.

functions.name: state
functions.what: Prints one state line: label, time, boot id, MemTotal, load, logins, marker file, processes per user.

functions.name: fail
functions.what: Prints `FAILED:` and the message, prints a state line, ends go2.sh with exit status 1.

functions.name: rxok
functions.what: Tests that `launches.txt` of the newest result folder of that name holds exactly one `rc` line, with status 0.

functions.name: waitidle
functions.what: Tests every 5 s, at most 180 times, whether the 1-minute load average is below 1.0. Stops the run after 15 min.
